books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Fort Sumter crisis as told in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 15, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.7. Dates, hours, and casualty figures verified against the National Park Service (nps.gov/apco/april-1861.htm) and the Battle of Fort Sumter record. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: Fort Sumter stood on an island in Charleston Harbor, one of the last federal forts still held in the seceded South. In April 1861 President Lincoln told South Carolina he would send food, but not men or arms, to the hungry garrison. Before the supply ships arrived, Confederate guns opened fire at 4:30 in the morning on April 12. After about thirty-four hours of bombardment, Major Robert Anderson surrendered the fort on April 13. No soldier was killed by the shelling. Two days later, on April 15, Lincoln called for 75,000 militiamen to put down the rebellion, and four more slave states — Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina — left the Union.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The passage most directly suggests that Lincoln's call for troops after Sumter had which unintended effect?

options.text: It drove four Upper South states into the Confederacy.
It persuaded the Deep South to return to the Union.
options.misconception: The Deep South had already seceded; the call pushed the Upper South out, not the Deep South back in.

options.text: It ended all secession in the border states.
options.misconception: Background: the border states stayed in the Union, but secession sentiment there did not simply end.

options.text: It stopped the fighting at Fort Sumter.
options.misconception: The fort had already surrendered on April 13, two days before the call.

rationales.A: The passage says four more slave states left the Union after the call for 75,000 militiamen. Background: Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina had refused to secede until Lincoln asked for troops to coerce the South.
rationales.B: The Deep South had already seceded; the call pushed the Upper South out, not the Deep South back in.
rationales.C: Background: the border states stayed in the Union, but secession sentiment there did not simply end.
rationales.D: The fort had already surrendered on April 13, two days before the call.
rationales.general:
1. The call was meant to put down a rebellion.
2. The Upper South read it as coercion of fellow slave states.
3. Background: Virginia's convention voted to secede on April 17, two days after the call.
4. A show of force can widen the very rebellion it means to crush.
Remember: watch what a response does to the undecided — they are the audience that matters.
